explicit_facts: Mark Taylor is EnronOnline (EOL) counsel, as Karen Lambert refers to him as 'Mark Taylor (EOL counsel)'.
Mark Taylor is involved in establishing the 'index' used to describe contracts and had a meeting with 'Mark D.' (Mark Dilworth) about what the index should look like.
Mark Taylor's preferred approach is that the General Terms and Conditions (GTC) taken together with the long description should result in a 'complete, unambiguous contract'.
Mark Taylor requested 'Revised Gas Option Language' from Taffy Milligan and circulated a revised version asking for comments.
Mark Taylor stated the revised gas option language works 'as long as the long description describes multi-month options as a series of multiple options.'
Mark Taylor is the point person who directs the review/approval of utility and government counterparties for online trading; Tana Jones notes 'Mark can override any decision I have made'.

Mark Taylor explained the difficulty of knowing which entities are regulated, citing that ENA is an 'unregulated' affiliate of a regulated utility (PGE), while other energy-services affiliates are 'nevertheless heavily regulated'.
Mark Taylor stated that draft product descriptions for Australian Power would need to be updated 'based on input from you and Mark Taylor' once the GTC is finalised.

Mark Taylor provided feedback on the Auction Procedures draft (from Sullivan & Cromwell / S&C), arguing a verifiable end time for the auction period is needed, and 'we need a verifiable end time for the Auction Period'.

Mark Taylor, in February 2000, explained to Bryan Seyfried that legal due-diligence for reference entities for EnronOnline 'will be a lengthier process than that which we were able to accomplish before the launch of the EnronCredit.com page'.
Mark Taylor pointed out that credit derivatives are not being offered in certain jurisdictions including Germany and Canada.
Mark Taylor confirmed that the earlier concern that credit derivatives could be considered insurance was resolved.
enron_taylor_forster_intl.short_summary: Mark Taylor, EnronOnline (EOL) counsel, worked through late 1999 and 2000 to build out the legal framework for EnronOnline's structured trading. He coordinated with David Forster on the GTCs, long descriptions, and the contract 'index,' preferring that the GTC plus long description together form a complete, unambiguous contract. He reviewed gas option language supplied by Taffy Milligan, worked to approve utility and government counterparties for online trading (noting that he can override staff decisions but relies on due diligence), and commented on auction procedure drafts from outside counsel S&C. As the Australian Power launch approached, Mark's legal input on the GTC was required, and he flagged that credit derivatives were not offered in Germany and Canada. He also worked on Password Agreements (PA) and ETA documents, insisting the PA stay a single page and that registration forms precede user IDs, while confirming earlier insurance-regulatory concerns about credit derivatives had been resolved.
enron_taylor_forster_intl.long_summary: Mark Taylor is EOL (EnronOnline) counsel at Enron. Early in the thread he is refining how contracts are described on the platform: after a morning meeting with Mark D. (Mark Dilworth) he notes an open item about what the 'Index' should look like and how much input the confirm desk has had, and explains his inclination that the index use the same language as the confirmation because the GTC combined with the long description should yield a 'complete, unambiguous contract.' Mark Dilworth agrees to follow up with Jennifer and Torrey before the 11 a.m. legal-team meeting. On gas options, Taffy Milligan sends Mark 'Revised Gas Option Language' at his request, and Mark says the language works for him as long as multi-month options are described as a series of multiple options. Mark is also the key attorney approving counterparties to trade online; Tana Jones explains that she can only decide within guidelines set by the attorneys and that 'Mark can override any decision I have made,' and she sends his note about utilities at his direction. Mark defends the difficulty of determining which entities are regulated, citing ENA as an 'unregulated' affiliate of PGE while many energy-service affiliates are still 'heavily regulated.' On the Australian power launch, drafts are loaded into the system and will be updated based on input from Mark once the GTC is finalised. For the credit-derivatives business Mark reviews auction procedures drafted (in a first draft) by S&C, favoring a verifiable end time for the auction period, and instructs that certain jurisdictions such as Germany and Canada are not yet covered. He confirms the insurance concern over credit derivatives was resolved. Regarding reference entities, Mark tells Bryan that EnronOnline's legal due-diligence will be lengthier than what was possible before EnronCredit.com launched. He also weighs in on Password Agreements and the ETA, advocating that the PA stay on a single page and that a completed registration form should precede issuance of a user ID and password. Later items include Mark being unwell in early June 2000 (per Tony Pryor, 'Taffy said you're under the weather'), reviewing a revised gas pipeline offering draft, agreeing to a Gross Error clause that makes the provision more bilateral, and, in April 2001, answering Dave Forster's questions about CFTC registration and hedge-fund counterparty tests: a fund that lets retail investors in (like Fidelity) needs $1,000,000,000 in assets, a true hedge fund limited to sophisticated investors needs $100,000,000, and the site remains unregistered ('we are a one-to-many site and are not yet subject to these rules').

qa.q: What role does Mark Taylor hold in this conversation?
qa.a: Mark Taylor is EnronOnline (EOL) counsel.
qa.evidence: Karen Lambert writes 'Mark Taylor (EOL counsel) requested that I coordinate directly with you because you are the point person gathering a complete set of OnLine GTC's.'

qa.q: What is Mark Taylor's preference regarding how the Index and long description should be structured?
qa.a: Mark Taylor prefers that the GTC taken together with the long description form a complete, unambiguous contract, and that the index use the same language currently used in the confirmation.
qa.evidence: Mark Taylor: 'My inclination was that the index should be the same language that we currently use in the confirmation on the theory that the GTC taken together with the long description should result in a complete, unambiguous contract.'

qa.q: Why does Mark Taylor say he agrees with keeping the Gross Error clause but wants it made reciprocal?
qa.a: Mark Taylor wants the provision to be more bilateral so that errors are not voidable only at Enron's election.
qa.evidence: After Dave Forster proposes reciprocal language, Mark responds 'That works to make it more bilateral. I think we still have the fundamental problem that it is a basically flawed concept.'

qa.q: In which jurisdictions was EnronOnline's credit derivatives product not being offered?
qa.a: Germany and Canada.
qa.evidence: Mark Taylor: 'There are still certain jurisdictions where we are not offering the product: Germany and Canada come to mind.'

qa.q: What asset threshold does a hedge fund limited to sophisticated investors need versus a fund that allows retail investors, according to Mark Taylor?
qa.a: A fund that allows investors like the public (a Fidelity-type fund) needs $1,000,000,000 in assets, while a hedge fund that limits investors to those meeting sophistication requirements needs $100,000,000.
qa.evidence: Mark Taylor: 'A fund group like Fidelity that allows my Mom to invest has to have $1,000,000,000 in assets. A true hedge fund that limits its investors to those meeting certain sophistication requirements only needs $100,000,000 in total assets.'

deductive: Mark Taylor reports into or coordinates closely with an EnronOnline/EOL launch team that includes David Forster, since Forster repeatedly seeks Mark's legal sign-off on GTCs, PAs, and product descriptions before launch dates are set.
Mark Taylor is senior to or has sign-off authority over the staff (e.g., Tana Jones) who approve online counterparties, since 'Mark can override any decision I have made'.
Because Mark is the EOL counsel, the trading platform cannot go live (e.g., Australian Power) until his legal inputs on the GTC and long descriptions are finalized.
inductive: Mark Taylor favors simplicity and document efficiency: he pushes to keep the Password Agreement to a single page and prefers language reuse rather than new drafting.

Mark Taylor is willing to accept drafting compromises that shift risk bilaterally, shown by his embrace of a reciprocal Gross Error clause and his tolerance of the counterparty's added liability-mitigation language.
Mark Taylor is pragmatic about commercial realities over legal purity, as when he calls the Gross Error concept 'basically flawed' but does not let drafting block the deal.

explicit_facts: Mark Taylor (at ECT) is the attorney reviewing and negotiating the ISDA documentation Enron proposed to send to IBJ (Industrial Bank of Japan).
Enron provided a draft ISDA schedule to IBJ, and IBJ's Yamato Konishi returned it amended by IBJ's legal desk and stated 'Part 6 on the schedule is needed to be deleted.'
IBJ stated the 'ISDA Credit support annex is not acceptable' and claimed 'we don't have internal system for concluding CSA with non-financial entity.'
Mark Taylor argued that IBJ is 'the most sophisticated Japanese player in the derivative market' and should be able to handle the CSA documentation.

Mark Taylor decided the CSA is 'an issue for Credit' and would forward it to John Suttle for input, noting a CSA 'is certainly not necessary to have a valid agreement but it is necessary if you want to insist on collateral.'

Mark Taylor insisted Enron keep Part 6 (Commodity Transaction provisions) in the master because deleting it would require adding language to each confirmation, making it 'more cumbersome to do business with that counterparty.'
Mark Taylor required that IBJ 'explain the changes rather than just sending us a mark-up' given the seriousness of their revisions.

Mark Taylor took firm positions on IBJ's revisions, e.g. refusing to expand defaults to Enron affiliates, insisting on netting payments per transaction (Part 4(f)) and rejecting 10 business days for confirming transactions (Part 5(e)).
IBJ raised that Enron had a loan from IBJ of roughly US$100,000,000.
Enron is the Calculation Agent under the proposed agreement, though John Viverito believed IBJ would make its own calculations to double-check Enron's.
enron_taylor_suttle_ibj_isda.short_summary: Mark Taylor (ECT/Houston) led Enron's negotiation of the ISDA master agreement documentation with IBJ (Industrial Bank of Japan) in late 2000. IBJ returned the draft schedule with revisions: it wanted Part 6 (Commodity Transaction provisions) deleted, refused the Credit Support Annex (CSA), and asked Enron to explain 'EDGAR.' Mark pushed back, arguing there is no downside to keeping language in the master, that deleting Part 6 would burden the back office for every confirmation, and that a CSA should be evaluated by Credit (John Suttle) while noting it is only needed if Enron insists on collateral. Mark insisted IBJ explain its changes rather than just send a mark-up, and took firm positions on default, set-off, confidentiality, market-maker location, and confirmation timing. IBJ countered that it has never done a CSA with a non-financial institution and that Enron owed it roughly US$100 million under a loan. Colleagues (John Viverito, John Suttle, Jonathan Whitehead, Tom Bruce-Jones) kept pushing for the CSA, while Mark's earlier argument that IBJ is 'the most sophisticated Japanese player in the derivative market' was cited within the team.
enron_taylor_suttle_ibj_isda.long_summary: Mark Taylor is the Enron (ECT/Houston) attorney responsible for the ISDA documentation being negotiated with IBJ, Japan's Industrial Bank of Japan, toward the end of 2000. The counterparty, via Yamato Konishi in IBJ Tokyo, signalled early that Part 6 of the schedule needs to be deleted (preferring terms be referred to in each confirmation), that the ISDA Credit Support Annex is 'not acceptable' because they claim to lack an internal system for CSAs with non-financial entities, and later that the word 'EDGAR' on page 4 is unclear. Mark responded that deleting Part 6 would force additional language into every confirmation, which the back office templates do not support, making it 'more cumbersome to do business with that counterparty'; he saw 'no down-side' to keeping the language in the master. He also noted the CSA is a Credit issue, forwarded it to John Suttle, and explained a CSA is not necessary for a valid agreement but is necessary if Enron wants to insist on collateral, adding it may actually be a burden if IBJ is the stronger credit. Mark argued that calling the counterparty unable to handle nonfinancial CSA documentation is 'disingenuous' and that IBJ, 'the most sophisticated Japanese player in the derivative market,' should handle both financial and non-financial entities. IBJ returned a full red-line with detailed positions (Part 1(a) affiliates, Part 1(g) merger termination, Part 4(f) netting limited to same transaction due to 'system incapability,' Part 5(a)/(c)/(e)/(g)/(j)/(n), and Part 6 still to be in confirmations), and noted Enron owes IBJ roughly US$100,000,000. Mark provided point-by-point responsive positions, insisting defaults not be expanded to all Enron affiliates, that per-transaction netting is required, that 10 business days is far too long ('we can not have certainty as to the terms of the transaction for two weeks!'), and that confidentiality must be preserved. Colleagues such as John Suttle (Credit) and Jonathan Whitehead continued to push the CSA, arguing IBJ simply does not want to sign one with a non-financial institution, while IBJ said it was 'not ready for running collateral operations'; the thread reflects an unresolved, sustained negotiation where Enron aims to keep the relationship going even if a CSA is not obtained.

qa.q: What is Mark Taylor's role in this negotiation?
qa.a: Mark Taylor is the Enron attorney reviewing and responding to IBJ's comments on the ISDA documentation, and the one whose legal positions the team relies on.
qa.evidence: John Viverito writes 'I will need to get his input regarding our most efficient going forward strategy' and forwards Mark's comments; Mark Taylor@ECT signs the detailed negotiation responses.

qa.q: Why does Mark Taylor oppose deleting Part 6 of the ISDA schedule?
qa.a: Because the provisions would then have to be added into each confirmation, which the back office templates are not set up for, making deals more cumbersome.
qa.evidence: Mark Taylor: 'as we would insist on the appropriate provisions being in the confirm in any event... it is also necessary if you want to insist on collateral' and 'If these provisions are not included here they will need to be included in each confirmation (a significant burden for our back office systems which are not set up for it).'

qa.q: What is Mark Taylor's view on the Credit Support Annex?
qa.a: He views the CSA as a Credit issue (to be decided by John Suttle), says it is not necessary for a valid agreement but is necessary if Enron wants to insist on collateral, and argues IBJ's systems objection is not credible.
qa.evidence: Mark Taylor: 'With respect to the CSA, that is an issue for Credit. I will forward this to John Suttle for his input. It is certainly not necessary to have a valid agreement but it is necessary if you want to insist on collateral... It strikes me as disingenuous to say that they don't have the internal systems for csa's with nonfinancial counterparties.'

qa.q: What counterparty fact did IBJ raise that complicated the CSA negotiation?
qa.a: That Enron had a loan from IBJ of roughly US$100,000,000.
qa.evidence: John Viverito: 'I note that IBJ also raised the point that Enron had a loan from IBJ of roughly US$ 100,000,000.'

deductive: Mark Taylor defers credit decisions (e.g. whether to insist on the CSA) to the Credit department (John Suttle), implying credit risk decisions sit outside Legal.

Because IBJ wants the relationship and fears delays, Enron can hold firm on terms (e.g. insisting on an explanation for mark-ups) without losing the deal, as IBJ pushed hard to 'conclude this process rapidly.'
The negotiation is unresolved as of the thread: IBJ still refuses the CSA, so any eventual trading with IBJ is contingent on either a CSA compromise or accepting trades without collateral.
inductive: Mark Taylor values clear, verifiable legal positions over speed: he insists IBJ 'explain the changes rather than just sending us a mark-up' and rejects vague language ('The language inserted is much to vague').
Mark Taylor is unwilling to let a counterparty gain one-sided advantage hidden in drafting: he insists on netting, confidentiality, and rejecting default-expansion across all affiliates.

Mark Taylor is a pragmatic negotiator who maintains firm positions but remains open to commercial reality, noting a CSA might be more of a burden than a benefit if the counterparty is the stronger credit.

explicit_facts: Louise Kitchen is Chief Operating Officer, Enron Americas, per her email signature block 'Louise Kitchen, Chief Operating Officer, Enron Americas.'
Louise Kitchen co-leads the Enron Americas trading staff group with John Lavorato, who addresses her as a joint coordinator and says 'Louise and I would like to get everyone together offsite.'
Louise Kitchen was on holiday, and John Lavorato jokingly scheduled the proposed offsite 'once Louise is back from holiday (just kidding).'

Louise Kitchen participated in evaluating/ranking the top traders (a 'schoolyard' ordering) based partly on P&L and future-leadership potential, and disagreed with John Lavorato about Chris Calger's rank, calling him 'a future leader of this organisation.'
Louise Kitchen recommended equity and options compensation for EES contributors, including Rogers Herndon ($500K total), Don Black ($500K), Jeff Richter ($200K), and Bernie Aucoin ($200K).

Louise Kitchen recommended dropping the old NGL group (propane/butane) that John Arnold 'picked up... from EGM,' because Enron lacked the systems, lawyers, and credit capacity to manage them, and would do so 'Unless I hear otherwise.'
Louise Kitchen negotiated with trading staff (e.g., Tim Belden) over retention, 2001 compensation security, and indemnification during a 'Newco' deal, and Belden apologized for hanging up on her.
Louise Kitchen coordinated the retention/options mechanics, telling Tim Belden it would be 'a memo or some form of written document indicating the people and total dollars needed to secure them.'
Louise Kitchen's Houston cell number is 713 530 0838 and she also gave a UK number 011447778757656.
enron_kitchen_lavorato_trading.short_summary: Louise Kitchen, Chief Operating Officer of Enron Americas, coordinated with John Lavorato in running the trading organization. Together they planned a group offsite at Beaver Creek and monthly staff meetings for everyone with P&L responsibility, after killing a planned offsite in December due to market volatility. Louise and John compared their rankings of the organization's top traders, with Louise arguing the list should weigh future leadership, and she recommended equity/options awards for EES contributors. As the business moved toward a 'Newco' deal, Louise negotiated with Tim Belden over his 2001 compensation and retention, and coordinated options/retention documentation. Louise also recommended dropping an NGL group Arnold had brought in because the organization lacked the systems, lawyers, and credit capacity to manage it, and she directed headcount and staffing decisions amid the restructuring.
enron_kitchen_lavorato_trading.long_summary: Louise Kitchen signs as Chief Operating Officer, Enron Americas, and is a central decision-maker in the trading organization that she runs alongside John Lavorato. After killing a planned offsite in December because of market volatility, John and Louise planned to bring the group that 'drives Enron's success' together for a late-June offsite (once Louise returns from holiday, John jokes) and to hold monthly staff meetings for everyone with P&L responsibility. Louise engaged in the evaluation process by ranking traders, and in a 'schoolyard' file she compared her ordering to John's: she argued Chris Calger should rank ahead of Benson and Zufferli because 'he's a future leader of this organisation,' and characterized John's ordering as 'very P&L based.' She recommended equity value plus options for EES contributors on the strength of their work on EES issues (Rogers Herndon $500K, Don Black $500K, Jeff Richter $200K, Bernie Aucoin $200K). In the run-up to a sale/newco, Louise negotiated with Tim Belden about securing 2001 compensation, 90-day retentions, and indemnification; Belden detailed a free option he was willing to give the buyer contingent on retention payments and indemnification of up to $4 million, apologized for hanging up on Louise, and asked her to reconsider. Louise described internal options mechanics as a written memo indicating 'the people and total dollars needed to secure them.' She also made portfolio decisions, recommending dropping the old NGL group (propane/butane) that John Arnold had picked up from EGM because there were no systems, lawyers, or credit capacity to manage them, and noted she was handling specific allocations (e.g., 'Steffes 50/50' and 'Nicolay 25/25'). She gave out her cell numbers (713 530 0838 and 011447778757656) and handled headcount and staffing coordination during the transition.

qa.q: What is Louise Kitchen's role and where does she sit in the organization?
qa.a: She is the Chief Operating Officer of Enron Americas.
qa.evidence: Her signature block reads 'Louise Kitchen, Chief Operating Officer, Enron Americas'.

qa.q: Who co-leads the trading group with Louise, and what gathering did they plan?
qa.a: John Lavorato co-led the group with her; they planned an offsite (held at Beaver Creek) and monthly staff meetings.
qa.evidence: John Lavorato: 'Louise and I would like to get everyone together offsite' and attendees write to 'John and Louise' about the 'Beaver Creek offsite.'

qa.q: What did Louise recommend doing with the old NGL group, and why?
qa.a: She recommended dropping them because Enron lacked the systems, lawyers, and credit capacity to manage them.
qa.evidence: Louise Kitchen: 'My recommendation is to drop them as we have no systems, lawyers, credit capacity to manage them. Unless I hear otherwise they will be gone.'

qa.q: What compensation awards did Louise propose for the EES team?
qa.a: Rogers Herndon and Don Black each $500K total (equity + options), and Jeff Richter and Bernie Aucoin each $200K.
qa.evidence: Louise Kitchen: 'Rogers Herndon $250K / $250K / $500K, Don Black $250K / $250K / $500K, Jeff Richter $100K / $100K / $200K, Bernie Aucoin $100K / $100K / $200K.'

qa.q: What was Tim Belden upset about in his dealings with Louise and John?
qa.a: He wanted assurances that 90-day retentions would be paid and that his 2001 compensation was secure, plus indemnification of 2001 comp up to $4 million, before giving the buyer a free option.
qa.evidence: Tim Belden: 'I need assurances that 90 day retentions will be paid... I am saying that a condition precedent for me is to negotiate a separate indemnification doc with the buyer' and 'indemnification of 2001 comp up to $4 million.'

deductive: Louise Kitchen is part of senior leadership equivalent to John Lavorato, given she co-directs the group and decides compensation and portfolio (hang/don't-hang) matters.
Louise Kitchen is empowered to grant equity and options to staff, implying she has authority over compensation banding within Enron Americas.

The 'Newco' transaction, retention, and 2001-comp security issues are interdependent: Belden's willingness to stay and give the buyer an option was contingent on resolving those compensation uncertainties.
Louise Kitchen is an executive who manages her calendar and travel, since a proposed meeting/offsite was deferred pending her return from holiday.
inductive: Louise values talent evaluation that looks beyond immediate P&L: she promotes Chris Calger because 'he's a future leader of this organisation' over a purely P&L-based ranking.
Louise is decisive and risk-averse about portfolio additions without infrastructure, recommending they 'drop them' when there are no systems, lawyers, or credit capacity.

Louise maintains informal rapport with her team (jokes in the schoolyard ordering, playful tone with Lavorato) while holding firm business positions, which helped defuse a tense negotiation with Tim Belden.

enron_shackleton_nelson_eci_guaranty.short_summary: Sara Shackleton, a documentation attorney at Enron North America Corp., managed the formation and brokerage documentation for Enron Credit Inc. (ECI), a new Delaware company created to take over ENA's U.S. debt trading. She directed the transfer of ENA's brokerage debt positions at Bear Stearns, Morgan Stanley, and Goldman Sachs into ECI accounts by end of February 2001, and oversaw assignment of the Securities Loan Agreement and the 'credit book' from ENA to ECI. Working with Senior Counsel Cheryl Nelson, Tom Doukas, Sheila Glover, and London-based Richard Sage, Sara drove execution of the account agreements and the replacement ENE guaranty (raised from USD25 million to USD100 million), set March 28 as the target execution date, and advised on arbitration provisions and repo authority under the ECI resolutions.
enron_shackleton_nelson_eci_guaranty.long_summary: Sara Shackleton, at Enron North America Corp., was the coordinator handling the legal documentation for the new Enron Credit Inc. (ECI), a Delaware corporation set up for U.S. debt trading currently handled by ENA. She instructed that ENA transfer its brokerage debt positions to ECI accounts at its 'favorites' — Bear Stearns, Morgan Stanley & Co. Inc., and Goldman Sachs & Co. — and flagged that assignment of positions was needed by the end of February 2001. She routed the 'sample package' (unanimous consent and authorized trader list) to Richard Sage in London and had Stephanie prepare three sets of assignment agreements. Sara proposed adding arbitration language for Morgan (a forum other than a contract market such as AAA, and limiting arbitrators' authority to award punitive/exemplary damages), which Senior Counsel Cheryl Nelson flagged may be unenforceable under NASD rules; Sara noted Morgan itself subsequently proposed similar language. Sara managed the transfer of the Securities Loan Agreement from ENA to ECI and the replacement ENE guaranty (rising from USD25 million to USD100 million in favor of Bear, Stearns), coordinated with Cheryl about officers being confirmed through the Enron Corp. corporate secretary's office, and set Wednesday, March 28, 2001 as the target execution date for the ECI customer agreement and assignment. She clarified the only agreement ENA was assigning was the Securities Loan Agreement, while ENA also assigned the 'credit book.' Later, on repos, she stated she was not certain the existing resolution covers repurchase/reverse-repurchase transactions and securities lending but would locate the proper Goldman contact, and she requested copies of the ECI resolutions/consents and Enron Credit Limited authorizations to determine which products ECI was authorized to trade.

qa.q: What is Sara Shackleton's professional role and location?
qa.a: She is a documentation/contracts attorney at Enron North America Corp., Houston (1400 Smith Street).
qa.evidence: Her signature block reads 'Sara Shackleton, Enron North America Corp., 1400 Smith Street, EB 3801a, Houston, Texas 77002, 713-853-5620.'

deductive: Sara Shackleton holds a senior documentation role and effectively project-manages the ECI formation, since she sets execution dates and directs Senior Counsel Cheryl Nelson, Stephanie, and Sheila Glover.
The ENA-to-ECI transfer is contingent on the brokerage account agreements and the ENE guaranty being executed simultaneously, so the counterparties are comfortable with the new legal entity.

The replacement guaranty (USD25M to USD100M) signals increased exposure/credit support being provided to Bear Stearns as the business moves to ECI.
inductive: Sara is detail-oriented and procedurally rigorous about documentation: she insists that assignment agreements, authorized trader lists, officer confirmations, and guaranties be properly executed and filed ('we should begin the documentation now').
Sara is proactive about unblocking deals: she chases status updates (asking Sheila and Tom to be advised mid-day) and follows up on files not located, coordinating with multiple parties in parallel.

Sara is commercially pragmatic: she was proven right on the need for the guaranty ('you thought I was kidding about needing the guaranty!'), showing she anticipates counterparty requirements based on experience.

enron_shackleton_bailey_isda_master.short_summary: Sara Shackleton coordinates Enron's financial master agreement (ISDA) documentation across multiple geographies. She is a key contact for approved ISDA documentation (referred to Brian Swinford for the CIESA interest-rate swap), manages the monthly Argentina/Brazil financial master-agreement schedule that lists the status of master agreements, and controls who is on the distribution.
